pos: v. (past tense of choose: took by preference; of God, elected)
etymology: Past tense of choose, Saxon ceosan. The Authorized Version uses the same past tense for the lifting of a man's eyes over a well-watered plain and for the eternal purpose of God toward a people — and the difference between the two is the difference between the flesh and grace.
biblical_def: Put the two great instances side by side. “Then Lot chose him all the plain of Jordan” (Gen 13:11) — a man lifted up his eyes, saw that it was well watered everywhere, and took it; and the plain he chose was Sodom. That is human choosing: by sight, for advantage, and ruinous. Against it stands Moses' account of Israel's existence: “because he loved thy fathers, therefore he chose their seed after them, and brought thee out in his sight with his mighty power out of Egypt” (Deu 4:37). Note the order, for it is the whole doctrine of unconditional election: He loved, therefore He chose, therefore He brought out. Nothing in the seed moved Him; Deuteronomy 7 says plainly that they were the fewest of all people. “Only the LORD had a delight in thy fathers to love them, and he chose their seed after them, even you above all people” (Deu 10:15). The cause of election lies in God's good pleasure, not in the thing chosen. David knew it of his own throne: the LORD “chose me before thy father, and before all his house” (2Sa 6:21), and the answer to Michal's contempt was not his dignity but God's choice. And Judges gives the counterfeit in five words: “They chose new gods; then was war in the gates” (Jdg 5:8). A people that does the choosing gets the war.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines choose as to pick out, to select from a number, to take by way of preference; and in theology, to elect — God having chosen his people to holiness.
webster_full: CHOOSE, v.t. To pick out; to select; to take by way of preference from two or more things offered.
1. To take in preference; to prefer.
2. In theology, to elect; to predestinate; to designate to a particular use or state.
ELECT, v.t. To choose; to select or take for an office or employment. In theology, to designate, choose or select as an object of mercy or favor.
scriptures: Deu 4:37
And because he loved thy fathers, therefore he chose their seed after them, and brought thee out in his sight with his mighty power out of Egypt;
Only the LORD had a delight in thy fathers to love them, and he chose their seed after them, even you above all people, as it is this day.
Then Lot chose him all the plain of Jordan; and Lot journeyed east: and they separated themselves the one from the other.
Jdg 5:8
They chose new gods; then was war in the gates: was there a shield or spear seen among forty thousand in Israel?
corruption_summary: Election is retold as God ratifying the choice of the sinner; Scripture puts the verb in God's mouth first.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest modern account of salvation makes the decisive verb the sinner's: God offers, man chooses, God responds. Deuteronomy 4:37 will not be read that way. Love, then choice, then deliverance — and the object of the choice is described everywhere in the same book as stiffnecked, rebellious, and the fewest of all peoples. Our Lord says it in the plainest possible words to men who had followed Him for years: Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you (Joh 15:16). This is not a denial that men choose; Lot chose, Israel chose new gods, and both choices were real and both were culpable. It is a denial that man's choosing is the ground of God's.

The second corruption is the conditional election that grants the word while emptying it — God chose those whose future faith He foresaw. That reverses cause and effect and re-establishes merit under a new name, since the foreseen faith is then the reason for the choosing and originates in the man. The confessional position is that God's election is of his mere free grace and love, without any other thing in the creature as a condition or cause moving him thereunto (LBCF 3.5), and that faith is the fruit of election rather than its ground: as many as were ordained to eternal life believed (Act 13:48).
roots_summary: Hebrew bachar (H977), to choose, to elect; Greek eklegomai (G1586), to pick out for oneself; ekloge (G1589), election.
roots_lines: Hebrew bachar (H977) — to choose, select, elect; the covenant verb of Deuteronomy 4:37, 7:6-8, 10:15.
Hebrew chashaq (H2836) — to be attached to, to delight in; Deuteronomy 10:15, the LORD had a delight in thy fathers — affection, not merit, as the cause.
Greek eklegomai (G1586) — to choose out for oneself; John 15:16, Ephesians 1:4, chosen in him before the foundation of the world.
Greek ekloge (G1589) — the election, the choosing; Romans 9:11, that the purpose of God according to election might stand.
Greek prohorizo (G4309) — to mark out beforehand, to predestinate; Ephesians 1:5, 11.
usage: “He loved… therefore he chose” — the order is the doctrine.
“Lot chose him all the plain of Jordan” — by sight, and it was Sodom.
“They chose new gods; then was war in the gates” — a people that does the choosing.

pos: v. (to live again; to restore to life, vigour or use)
etymology: Latin revivere, to live again, from re- and vivere. In the Authorized Version the subject of the verb is almost always God, and its object is almost always something already dead, burnt or crushed.
biblical_def: Every biblical use of revive assumes that the thing to be revived cannot revive itself. “Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?” (Psa 85:6) — a prayer, addressed to God, in the passive of the people. Habakkuk prays the same way in a darker hour: “O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years… in wrath remember mercy” (Hab 3:2), and note that the work to be revived is God's own, not the prophet's programme. Isaiah names the two men God comes to: He dwells in the high and holy place, “with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones” (Isa 57:15). Hosea gives the promise its resurrection shape — “After two days will he revive us: in the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight” (Hos 6:2) — and the church has always heard the third day in it. Even Sanballat's sneer uses the word rightly: “will they revive the stones out of the heaps of the rubbish which are burned?” (Neh 4:2). He meant it as mockery; it is exactly what God does. Burnt stones, a crushed spirit, a dead people, a forgotten work — these are the materials of revival, and the verb belongs to God alone.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines revive as to return to life, to recover new life or vigor; and transitively, to bring again to life, to quicken, to reanimate.
webster_full: REVIVE, v.i. To return to life; to recover life.
1. To recover new life or vigor; to be reanimated after depression.
REVIVE, v.t. To bring again to life; to reanimate.
2. To recover from a state of neglect or oblivion; as, to revive letters or learning.
3. To renew; to bring into action after a suspension; as, to revive a controversy.
scriptures: For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones.
Psa 85:6
Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?
Hab 3:2
O LORD, I have heard thy speech, and was afraid: O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy.
Hos 6:2
After two days will he revive us: in the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight.
corruption_summary: Revival has been turned into a technique and a calendar date; Scripture keeps it a sovereign act prayed for, not produced.
corruption_paragraphs: Since the nineteenth century the noun revival has drifted from something God sends to something a church schedules — the new measures of Charles Finney, the anxious bench, the protracted meeting, the machinery calibrated to produce decisions. Finney said outright that a revival is not a miracle but the right use of the constituted means, and generations of American evangelicalism have organized around that sentence. Psalm 85 and Habakkuk 3 pray against it. The people cannot revive themselves; they ask. The verb has God for its subject in nearly every biblical instance, and where the machinery produces excitement without regeneration it has produced nothing that will stand.

The corrective is Isaiah 57:15, which tells the honest seeker exactly where God comes: to the contrite and to the humble. That is not a technique but it is a condition, and it is one no promotion can manufacture — a crushed spirit over sin. The old Reformed pastors prayed for revival, preached the word plainly, kept the ordinances, and waited; and when God came, the fruit was repentance and reformation of life rather than a crowd. Revive thy work is still the right prayer, and it is still addressed upward.
roots_summary: Hebrew chayah (H2421), to live, to keep alive, to revive; Piel, to make alive; dakka' (H1793), contrite, crushed.
roots_lines: Hebrew chayah (H2421) — to live; in the causative stems, to give life, to preserve alive, to revive; Psalm 85:6, Habakkuk 3:2, Hosea 6:2.
Hebrew dakka' (H1793) — crushed, contrite, beaten to dust; Isaiah 57:15, the heart God comes to revive.
Hebrew shaphal (H8217) — low, humble; the spirit revived in the same verse.
Greek zoopoieo (G2227) — to make alive, to quicken; John 5:21, Romans 8:11, 1 Corinthians 15:45.
Greek anazao (G326) — to live again; Romans 7:9, Luke 15:24, of the prodigal — he was dead, and is alive again.
usage: “Wilt thou not revive us again” — a prayer, not a plan.
“Revive thy work in the midst of the years” — the work is His.
“Revive the stones out of the heaps of the rubbish” — meant as mockery, and true.

pos: v. (to set right by discipline; to chastise in measure)
etymology: Latin corrigere, to make straight, from cor- and regere, to rule or direct. The English keeps the idea of straightening a thing that has bent, which is exactly the Hebrew use: correction is aimed at a crooked course, not at the destruction of the one corrected.
biblical_def: Jeremiah supplies the doctrine of this word in three sentences. First, the self-executing kind: “Thine own wickedness shall correct thee, and thy backslidings shall reprove thee” (Jer 2:19) — sin is its own schoolmaster, and God often needs no other rod than the natural harvest of the thing a man wanted. Second, the prayer of a man who knows he needs it: “O LORD, correct me, but with judgment; not in thine anger, lest thou bring me to nothing” (Jer 10:24). He does not ask to be spared correction; he asks for it in judgment rather than in wrath, which is precisely the distinction between fatherly chastisement and penal justice. Third, the promise: “I will correct thee in measure, and will not leave thee altogether unpunished” (Jer 30:11). In measure — weighed, limited, proportioned to the child and not to the offence in strict justice, because the strict justice fell at Calvary. The same word governs the home: “Correct thy son, and he shall give thee rest; yea, he shall give delight unto thy soul” (Pro 29:17), and Proverbs 23:13 forbids withholding it. And Psalm 94:10 settles the right of the Corrector: “He that chastiseth the heathen, shall not he correct?”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines correct as to make right, to rectify what is wrong; and to chastise, to punish for the purpose of amendment.
webster_full: CORRECT, v.t. To make right; to rectify; to bring to the standard of truth, justice or propriety.
1. To chastise; to punish for faults or deviations from moral rectitude; to discipline.
2. To obviate or remove whatever is wrong or inconvenient; to counteract, as an ill quality.
CORRECTION, n. Punishment; discipline; chastisement; that which corrects.
scriptures: O LORD, correct me, but with judgment; not in thine anger, lest thou bring me to nothing.

For I am with thee, saith the LORD, to save thee: though I make a full end of all nations whither I have scattered thee, yet will I not make a full end of thee: but I will correct thee in measure, and will not leave thee altogether unpunished.
Jer 2:19

Thine own wickedness shall correct thee, and thy backslidings shall reprove thee: know therefore and see that it is an evil thing and bitter, that thou hast forsaken the LORD thy God, and that my fear is not in thee, saith the Lord GOD of hosts.
Correct thy son, and he shall give thee rest; yea, he shall give delight unto thy soul.
corruption_summary: Correction of children is now widely reclassified as harm; Proverbs makes withholding it the cruelty.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant framework treats parental correction as a risk to be minimized, and reaches for the language of harm as the primary moral category. Scripture's categories are different and older: a child left uncorrected is not thereby protected but abandoned, because folly is bound in his heart and something must drive it out. Withhold not correction from the child (Pro 23:13) is a command to parents, and the promise attached to obeying it is rest and delight in the home. This is not license for anger. The very same Bible forbids provoking children to wrath, and the model of correction it gives is Jeremiah 30:11 — measured, purposeful, never to destruction, always aimed at restoring.

The deeper corruption is theological: a God who does not correct. Where fatherly chastisement is dropped from the doctrine of God, believers read every affliction either as divine anger or as meaningless accident, and both readings crush them. Hebrews 12 gives the third and true reading: whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and the son not chastened is the son not owned. Jeremiah's prayer is the right one — not spare me but correct me with judgment.
roots_summary: Hebrew yasar (H3256), to chastise, instruct, correct; musar (H4148), discipline, instruction; Greek paideuo (G3811), to train a child by discipline.
roots_lines: Hebrew yasar (H3256) — to discipline, chasten, instruct by correction; Jeremiah 10:24, 30:11, Proverbs 29:17.
Hebrew musar (H4148) — correction, discipline, instruction; the noun that runs through Proverbs 1-9.
Hebrew yakach (H3198) — to reprove, argue, set right; Jeremiah 2:19, thy backslidings shall reprove thee.
Greek paideuo (G3811) — to instruct a child, to chastise; Hebrews 12:6-10, 1 Corinthians 11:32.
Greek epanorthosis (G1882) — correction, setting straight again; 2 Timothy 3:16, profitable for correction.
usage: “Correct me, but with judgment; not in thine anger” — the believer's exact request.
“I will correct thee in measure” — weighed, limited, fatherly.
“Thine own wickedness shall correct thee” — sin as its own schoolmaster.

pos: v. (to hold back; to keep from giving or doing)
etymology: From with in its old sense of against or back, and hold. To withhold is not merely to fail to give but to keep back something that was on its way — which is why Scripture treats it as an act, and judges it.
biblical_def: Two promises and two commands carry this word. The promise: “For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly” (Psa 84:11). The comfort of that verse lies entirely in the word good. God withholds a great deal from His people, and the psalm does not deny it; it says that what He withholds is not good for them, on His judgment of good and not theirs. The prayer that answers it is David's: “Withhold not thou thy tender mercies from me, O LORD” (Psa 40:11). Then the commands, and both are about the hand. “Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it” (Pro 3:27) — a rebuke of the delayed wage, the deferred kindness, the good that is owed and postponed because postponement is cheap. And “Withhold not correction from the child” (Pro 23:13), where the good withheld is the painful kind. Ecclesiastes adds the labourer's form of it: “in the evening withhold not thine hand: for thou knowest not whether shall prosper” (Ecc 11:6). The pattern is consistent. God withholds by wisdom; man withholds by sloth, fear or greed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines withhold as to hold back, to restrain, to keep from action; and to retain, to keep back, not to grant.
webster_full: WITHHOLD, v.t. To hold back; to restrain; to keep from action.
1. To retain; to keep back; not to grant; as, to withhold assent to a proposition.
2. To keep; to maintain in possession; as, to withhold the wages of the hireling.
WITHHOLDEN, pp. Held back; restrained; kept from grant or exercise.
scriptures: For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly.
Pro 3:27
Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it.
Withhold not thou thy tender mercies from me, O LORD: let thy lovingkindness and thy truth continually preserve me.
Ecc 11:6
In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand: for thou knowest not whether shall prosper, either this or that, or whether they both shall be alike good.
corruption_summary: Psalm 84:11 is quoted as a promise of getting what one wants; the psalm makes God the judge of what is good.
corruption_paragraphs: No good thing will he withhold has been pressed into service as a guarantee of prosperity, health and the granting of desires, chiefly by the health-and-wealth teachers but also, more quietly, by ordinary believers doing their sums in the dark. The verse says something better and harder. It does not promise that God will withhold nothing; it promises that He will withhold no good thing, and it reserves to Him the determination of what is good. Paul asked three times for the thorn to be removed and was refused, and the refusal was the gift. A promise read the popular way collapses the first time a godly man buries a child; read as written, it survives the grave.

The command side is where the church has more to answer for. Proverbs 3:27 forbids the delay of good that is due and in the power of the hand — the unpaid worker, the unvisited widow, the reconciliation put off another year. James 5:4 says the hire kept back by fraud crieth, and the cries have entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth. Withholding is not passivity in Scripture; it is an act with a plaintiff.
roots_summary: Hebrew mana' (H4513), to withhold, keep back; chasak (H2820), to restrain, spare; Greek apostereo (G650), to defraud, to keep back what is owed.
roots_lines: Hebrew mana' (H4513) — to withhold, hold back, refuse; Psalm 84:11, Proverbs 3:27.
Hebrew chasak (H2820) — to restrain, hold back, spare; Proverbs 23:13, withhold not correction; Genesis 22:12, thou hast not withheld thy son.
Hebrew kala' (H3607) — to shut up, restrain; Psalm 40:11, withhold not thy tender mercies.
Greek apostereo (G650) — to defraud, to keep back wrongfully; James 5:4, the hire kept back by fraud.
Greek katecho (G2722) — to hold down, to restrain; 2 Thessalonians 2:6-7, of what withholdeth.
usage: “No good thing will he withhold” — and He decides what is good.
“Withhold not good from them to whom it is due” — when the hand can do it now.
“In the evening withhold not thine hand” — sow twice; you do not know which prospers.

pos: v. (in the Authorized Version: to approve, to sanction, to consent to as right — not merely to permit)
etymology: From Latin allaudare, to praise, crossed in English with allocare, to place or assign. The seventeenth-century sense that dominates the Authorized Version is the first: to allow a thing is to approve it, to give it your voice, which is why Romans 7:15 cannot be read with the modern meaning.
biblical_def: This is one of the words a modern reader will certainly misread unless he is warned. “For that which I do I allow not: for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I” (Rom 7:15). Paul is not saying that he does not permit his own actions, which would be nonsense; he is saying he does not approve them — the Greek is ginosko, to know or acknowledge, and the sense is that the regenerate man refuses to own the sin he still commits. That is the mark of the new nature: not sinlessness, but the settled disowning of the sin. Our Lord uses the word the same way against the scribes: “ye bear witness that ye allow the deeds of your fathers: for they indeed killed them, and ye build their sepulchres” (Luk 11:48). Building a prophet's tomb while sharing his murderers' heart is not permission, it is endorsement, and it is the charge. Paul before Felix uses it of shared confession: the resurrection is a hope “which they themselves also allow” (Act 24:15) — the Pharisees granted it, owned it, held it with him. To allow, in this Book, is to say amen to a thing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines allow first as to grant, give or yield; and second as to approve, to justify, to sanction — citing Romans 7:15 for the sense of approbation.
webster_full: ALLOW, v.t. To grant, give or yield; as, to allow a servant his liberty.
1. To admit; as, to allow the truth of a proposition.
2. To approve, justify or sanction. Ye allow the deeds of your fathers. Luke 11.
3. To afford; to grant; to permit; to suffer to be done.
ALLOWANCE, n. Approbation; sanction; license.
scriptures: Rom 7:15
For that which I do I allow not: for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I.
Truly ye bear witness that ye allow the deeds of your fathers: for they indeed killed them, and ye build their sepulchres.
And have hope toward God, which they themselves also allow, that there shall be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust.
corruption_summary: Read with the modern sense of “permit,” Romans 7:15 becomes an excuse for sin instead of the mark of a new heart.
corruption_paragraphs: A reader who imports today's meaning into Romans 7:15 gets a Paul who cannot help himself and is therefore not responsible — the verse becomes a shrug. The seventeenth-century sense gives the opposite. Paul says he does not approve what he does; the sin is committed and simultaneously disowned, hated, refused a vote. That refusal is precisely what the unregenerate man cannot produce and what the indwelling Spirit does produce. Romans 7 is not a permission slip; it is the anatomy of a war in a man who has been made new and is not yet made perfect.

The Luke 11 use guards the other flank. The scribes did nothing to the prophets; they merely built the sepulchres and approved. Scripture treats approval as participation — who knowing the judgment of God… not only do the same, but have pleasure in them that do them (Rom 1:32). In an age whose chief public act is the giving and withholding of approval, that verse is unnervingly current: a man is answerable for what he applauds, and building the monument can be its own confession.
roots_summary: Greek ginosko (G1097), to know, acknowledge, own; suneudokeo (G4909), to consent, to approve together with; dokimazo (G1381), to test and approve.
roots_lines: Greek ginosko (G1097) — to know, to recognize, to acknowledge as one's own; Romans 7:15, rendered allow in the sense of own or approve.
Greek suneudokeo (G4909) — to think well of together, to consent to; Luke 11:48, of consenting to the fathers' deeds; Acts 8:1, Saul was consenting unto his death.
Greek prosdechomai (G4327) — to receive, to accept, to look for; Acts 24:15, of the hope the Pharisees also owned.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to prove, to test, to approve after testing; Romans 12:2, 1 Thessalonians 2:4.
Greek euarestos (G2101) — well-pleasing, acceptable; the standard by which a thing may rightly be allowed.
usage: “That which I do I allow not” — approve not, and there is the new heart.
“Ye allow the deeds of your fathers” — approval counted as participation.
“Which they themselves also allow” — a hope owned in common.

pos: v. (to lay one thing to another; in Scripture, to bend the heart toward wisdom)
etymology: Latin applicare, to fold or fasten to, from ad and plicare, to fold. The literal picture is of laying one thing against another until it adheres — and in every biblical occurrence the thing applied is the heart.
biblical_def: The word occurs four times in the Authorized Version and the object is the same every time: the heart. “So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom” (Psa 90:12). Moses, in the psalm about the shortness of life under wrath, asks not for more days but for a heart laid against wisdom in the days that remain. Proverbs repeats the counsel three times over, and always as a deliberate act with a bodily image attached: “incline thine ear unto wisdom, and apply thine heart to understanding” (Pro 2:2); “Bow down thine ear, and hear the words of the wise, and apply thine heart unto my knowledge” (Pro 22:17); “Apply thine heart unto instruction, and thine ears to the words of knowledge” (Pro 23:12). Ear bowed, heart applied. Wisdom in Scripture is never absorbed passively by exposure; it is taken by a man who leans toward it on purpose, day after day, as a workman lays his rule against the timber. This is the doctrine of the means of grace in miniature. God gives wisdom sovereignly — the LORD giveth wisdom (Pro 2:6) — and He gives it to the man who cries after it, searcheth for it as for hid treasure, and applies his heart. The sovereignty does not excuse the leaning; it is the reason the leaning is not wasted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines apply as to lay on, to put one thing to another; and figuratively, to fix the mind, to engage and employ the attention with steadiness.
webster_full: APPLY, v.t. To lay on; to put one thing to another; as, to apply a plaster to a wound.
1. To use or employ for a particular purpose, or in a particular case.
2. To fix the mind; to engage and employ with attention. Apply thy heart to instruction. Proverbs 23.
APPLY, v.i. To suit; to agree; to have some connection or reference.
scriptures: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
Pro 2:2
So that thou incline thine ear unto wisdom, and apply thine heart to understanding;
Bow down thine ear, and hear the words of the wise, and apply thine heart unto my knowledge.
Apply thine heart unto instruction, and thine ears to the words of knowledge.
corruption_summary: “Application” has come to mean life tips appended to a text; Scripture means the heart laid against wisdom.
corruption_paragraphs: Preaching has largely reduced application to a list of practical steps tacked to the end of an exposition, and hearers have learned to wait for it as the useful part. The biblical verb runs the other way. It is not the preacher applying the text to the hearer's week; it is the hearer applying his own heart to the wisdom of God, ear bowed, over years. A sermon full of steps and empty of God will produce industrious men who never lean; a sermon that shows God truly will produce men who cannot help leaning. The Puritans understood the difference and called their applications uses — uses of the doctrine, not substitutes for it.

The second thing to recover is Psalm 90:12's reason for applying the heart: the days are numbered. Moses grounds the pursuit of wisdom in mortality, and modern life is arranged to keep mortality out of view. A man who has genuinely reckoned that his years are seventy, or by reason of strength eighty, and that they are soon cut off, has the strongest possible motive to lay his heart against something that will outlast them. That reckoning is the beginning of the application.
roots_summary: Hebrew bo' (H935) in the causative, to bring in; natah (H5186), to stretch out, incline; shith (H7896), to set or apply the heart.
roots_lines: Hebrew natah (H5186) — to stretch out, to incline, to bend; Proverbs 2:2, incline thine ear; Proverbs 22:17, bow down thine ear.
Hebrew shith (H7896) — to put, set, apply; Proverbs 22:17, apply thine heart unto my knowledge.
Hebrew bo' (H935) — to come, to bring; Psalm 90:12, that we may bring in a heart of wisdom.
Hebrew leb (H3820) — the heart, the seat of mind, will and affection; the object applied in all four verses.
Greek prosecho (G4337) — to hold the mind toward, to attend to; Hebrews 2:1, we ought to give the more earnest heed.
usage: “That we may apply our hearts unto wisdom” — the request of a man counting days.
“Bow down thine ear… and apply thine heart” — posture, then affection.
“Apply thine heart unto instruction” — wisdom is leaned toward, not absorbed.

pos: adv. (continually, without interruption; in Scripture, of God's regard and of man's unrelenting anger)
etymology: Latin perpetuus, continuous, uninterrupted, from per and petere, to go through. The Authorized Version uses the adverb three times, twice of the eyes and heart of God upon His house, and once of a brother's wrath that would not stop.
biblical_def: Twice God says of the temple: “mine eyes and mine heart shall be there perpetually” (1Ki 9:3; 2Ch 7:16). The words are worth weighing separately. Eyes — His constant regard, the attention that never lapses. Heart — His affection, so that the place is not merely watched but loved. And perpetually — without interruption, not in seasons of favour alternating with seasons of absence. That is the promise on which every prayer toward the house in Solomon's dedication rests, and the New Testament transfers it without loss: the temple is now a people, builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit, and the eyes and heart are there perpetually still. The third use is the exact inversion, and it is chilling: of Edom, “he did pursue his brother with the sword, and did cast off all pity, and his anger did tear perpetually, and he kept his wrath for ever” (Amo 1:11). The same adverb, the same unbroken continuity — but of a hatred. Esau's descendants nursed a grievance against Jacob's for a thousand years and God finally judged it. The word therefore measures two permanences: God's settled love toward His dwelling place, and man's settled refusal to forgive his brother. Both are described as never letting go.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines perpetually as constantly, continually, incessantly; applied to that which has no intermission.
webster_full: PERPETUALLY, adv. Constantly; continually; applied to things which proceed without intermission.
PERPETUAL, a. Never ceasing; continuing forever in future time; destined to be eternal.
1. Continuing or continued without intermission; uninterrupted; as a perpetual stream.
2. Everlasting; enduring; as a perpetual covenant; a perpetual statute.
scriptures: And the LORD said unto him, I have heard thy prayer and thy supplication, that thou hast made before me: I have hallowed this house, which thou hast built, to put my name there for ever; and mine eyes and mine heart shall be there perpetually.
For now have I chosen and sanctified this house, that my name may be there for ever: and mine eyes and mine heart shall be there perpetually.
Amo 1:11

Thus saith the LORD; For three transgressions of Edom, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because he did pursue his brother with the sword, and did cast off all pity, and his anger did tear perpetually, and he kept his wrath for ever:
corruption_summary: A grudge is now called boundaries or accountability; Amos calls perpetual anger against a brother a judged transgression.
corruption_paragraphs: Edom's sin in Amos 1:11 is not that he was wronged — Jacob genuinely wronged Esau — but that he kept the wrath, tearing perpetually, casting off all pity. Our own vocabulary has grown generous toward exactly this: the permanent estrangement is renamed as a boundary, the refusal to forgive as accountability, the cultivated grievance as processing. Some separations are lawful and even required, and Scripture provides for them. But it never provides for the perpetual anger itself. The unforgiving servant of Matthew 18 was delivered to the tormentors, and the sentence is attached to a warning that our Lord did not soften.

Set against it is the mercy of the other two verses. God's eyes and heart are perpetually upon His house — and He said it to Solomon, whose house would in time be defiled, whose kingdom would be torn, and whose temple would be burned. The perpetuity was not conditioned on the building's standing. That is the ground on which a man forgives his brother: he has been regarded perpetually by One who had every right to look away.
roots_summary: Hebrew kol-hayyamim, all the days; netsach (H5331), perpetuity, unending duration; 'ad (H5703), for ever.
roots_lines: Hebrew kol-hayyamim — all the days, continually; 1 Kings 9:3 and 2 Chronicles 7:16, of God's eyes and heart upon the house.
Hebrew netsach (H5331) — perpetuity, enduring; Amos 1:11, his anger did tear perpetually.
Hebrew 'ebrah (H5678) — overflowing rage, wrath; the wrath Edom kept for ever.
Hebrew rachamim (H7356) — compassions, tender mercies; what Edom cast off.
Greek diapantos (G1275) — continually, through all; Luke 24:53, Hebrews 13:15, of praise offered continually.
usage: “Mine eyes and mine heart shall be there perpetually” — regard and affection, unbroken.
“His anger did tear perpetually” — the same word, of a grudge.
“He kept his wrath for ever” — and God kept an account of it.

pos: adv. (in the Authorized Version: firmly, steadfastly, with unwavering assertion — not merely frequently)
etymology: Latin constans, standing firm, from con and stare, to stand. The seventeenth-century adverb means with constancy — steadfastly, immovably — and not, as today, at frequent intervals. Every occurrence turns on that difference.
biblical_def: Three occurrences, and the modern sense misreads all three. Rhoda, told she was mad for saying Peter stood at the gate, “constantly affirmed that it was even so” (Act 12:15) — not that she repeated herself often, but that she would not be moved off her testimony by a room full of praying adults who did not believe their own prayers had been answered. Proverbs contrasts the two kinds of witness: “A false witness shall perish: but the man that heareth speaketh constantly” (Pro 21:28) — the man who actually heard can hold his ground under pressure, because he is not maintaining a story but reporting a fact. And Paul charges Titus: “This is a faithful saying, and these things I will that thou affirm constantly, that they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works” (Tit 3:8). The minister is to state the gospel steadfastly, immovably, without hedging — and the stated purpose is practical: that believers should be careful to maintain good works. Doctrine affirmed constantly produces lives ordered accordingly. Doctrine offered tentatively produces nothing, because nobody builds a house on a sentence its speaker will not stand behind.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines constantly as firmly, steadfastly; and gives constancy as fixedness, immutability, steady adherence to purpose or principle.
webster_full: CONSTANTLY, adv. Firmly; steadfastly; invariably; continually.
CONSTANT, a. Fixed; firm; opposed to fluid.
1. Steady in affection or purpose; not fickle; as a constant friend.
2. Perseverance in attachment; as constancy in love.
CONSTANCY, n. Fixedness; immutability; a standing firm in purpose or opinion.
scriptures: Tit 3:8

This is a faithful saying, and these things I will that thou affirm constantly, that they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable unto men.
And they said unto her, Thou art mad. But she constantly affirmed that it was even so. Then said they, It is his angel.
A false witness shall perish: but the man that heareth speaketh constantly.
corruption_summary: Confident assertion of doctrine is now read as arrogance; Paul commands ministers to affirm constantly.
corruption_paragraphs: The prevailing style of religious speech is provisional: the qualification before the claim, the softening after it, the studied refusal to say a thing plainly in case someone should think one certain. Titus 3:8 commands the opposite of a minister — affirm constantly — and gives a pastoral reason rather than a combative one. People order their lives by what they can lean on. A congregation fed on hedged assertions will hedge its obedience to match. This is not a licence for brashness about matters Scripture leaves open; constancy in the faithful saying is exactly proportioned to the plainness of the revelation.

Rhoda's scene is the lay version and deserves its place. A servant girl held to what she had seen against the unanimous verdict of the praying church, and she was right and they were wrong. The one who has actually heard, Proverbs says, speaks constantly — the confidence is not in himself but in the fact. A believer who has met the risen Christ in His word need not be talked out of it by a roomful of people who cannot believe their own prayers were answered.
roots_summary: Greek diischurizomai (G1340), to affirm strongly, to insist; diabebaioomai (G1226), to affirm confidently; lanetsach (H5331), unto perpetuity, of steadfast speech.
roots_lines: Greek diischurizomai (G1340) — to lean on thoroughly, to affirm confidently; Acts 12:15 of Rhoda, Luke 22:59 of the man who accused Peter.
Greek diabebaioomai (G1226) — to affirm strongly, to assert steadfastly; Titus 3:8, 1 Timothy 1:7.
Greek pistos ho logos — the faithful saying; the formula Paul uses five times in the Pastorals to mark a settled gospel summary.
Hebrew netsach (H5331) — enduringly, unto the end; Proverbs 21:28, the true witness speaks so.
Hebrew 'ed sheqarim (H5707, H8267) — a witness of lies, a false witness; the man Proverbs sets against him.
usage: “She constantly affirmed that it was even so” — and she was right.
“These things I will that thou affirm constantly” — and then, good works.
“The man that heareth speaketh constantly” — because he is reporting, not maintaining.

pos: n. (duration; persistence in a course; the state of going on)
etymology: Latin continuare, to join without break. In the Authorized Version continuance attaches to four things: plagues, the days written in God's book, the sinner's hope, and the well-doing that seeks glory and honour and immortality.
biblical_def: “To them who by patient continuance in well doing seek for glory and honour and immortality, eternal life” (Rom 2:7). Paul is stating the law's own terms in an argument that will end by proving no man meets them, and the phrase remains exact for those who are in Christ: the marks of the saved are not a single moment but a patient continuance. Perseverance is not a second work added to salvation; it is the shape salvation takes over a life. Psalm 139 gives the ground of it in the most tender verse in the psalter about the unborn: “in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them” (Psa 139:16) — the days of a man's forming, and by extension all his days, written before one of them existed. Continuance is possible because the days were written. The word also carries judgment: the plagues of the disobedient are “of long continuance” (Deu 28:59), twice in one verse, the horror being precisely the duration. And Isaiah 64:5 sets the hinge: God meets the man that rejoiceth and worketh righteousness, “in those is continuance, and we shall be saved.” Continuance in God's ways is the evidence, and the salvation is the gift.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines continuance as a holding on or remaining in a particular state; perseverance; duration; and abode in a place.
webster_full: CONTINUANCE, n. A holding on or remaining in a particular state, or in a course or series.
1. Perseverance. How is it that thou wilt not continue in well doing?
2. Duration; lastingness; as the continuance of rain.
3. Abode; residence; as, during our continuance in Spain.
scriptures: Rom 2:7
To them who by patient continuance in well doing seek for glory and honour and immortality, eternal life:
Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect; and in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them.
Isa 64:5
Thou meetest him that rejoiceth and worketh righteousness, those that remember thee in thy ways: behold, thou art wroth; for we have sinned: in those is continuance, and we shall be saved.
Then the LORD will make thy plagues wonderful, and the plagues of thy seed, even great plagues, and of long continuance, and sore sicknesses, and of long continuance.
corruption_summary: Assurance is offered on a past decision alone; Scripture makes patient continuance the evidence of the thing decided.
corruption_paragraphs: A great deal of modern evangelism secures assurance to a recorded moment — a card, a prayer, a date — and treats any later question about continuance as doubt of God's promise. Romans 2:7 and the whole New Testament press the other way. He that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved (Mat 24:13); they went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us (1Jo 2:19). The doctrine is not that perseverance earns salvation, but that genuine salvation perseveres, and that a life which does not continue has given evidence about what the moment was.

The opposite error is to make continuance the ground of confidence, so that a believer measures his standing by his consistency and is therefore never at rest. Psalm 139:16 answers it: the days were written in God's book before there was one of them. The perseverance of the saints is the persevering of God with the saints — he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ (Php 1:6). Continue, then, because you are held; do not conclude that you are held only because you continued.
roots_summary: Greek hupomone (G5281), patient endurance under load; Hebrew yom (H3117), day; 'olam (H5769), long duration.
roots_lines: Greek hupomone (G5281) — a remaining under, patient endurance; Romans 2:7, patient continuance in well doing; Hebrews 10:36, ye have need of patience.
Greek aphtharsia (G861) — incorruption, immortality; the thing sought in Romans 2:7.
Hebrew yamim (H3117) — days; Psalm 139:16, the days fashioned and written before one of them was.
Hebrew ne'eman (H539) — firm, faithful, enduring; Deuteronomy 28:59, plagues of long continuance (literally, faithful — sicknesses that keep their appointment).
Greek emmeno (G1696) — to remain in, to abide by; Acts 14:22, Galatians 3:10.
usage: “By patient continuance in well doing” — not a moment but a shape.
“Which in continuance were fashioned” — the days written before there was one.
“Of long continuance” — twice in a verse, and the duration is the horror.

pos: n. (an ordering or direction; in the Authorized Version, chiefly the word of a man by which a matter is settled)
etymology: From appoint, Old French apointier, to arrange or settle. The Hebrew idiom behind three of the occurrences is literally at the mouth of — a thing done at the mouth of Aaron, at the mouth of Absalom — so that an appointment in Scripture is a spoken order that stands.
biblical_def: The Hebrew phrase rendered appointment is literally at the mouth of, and the four occurrences show what a mouth can order. Holy service: “At the appointment of Aaron and his sons shall be all the service of the sons of the Gershonites, in all their burdens” (Num 4:27) — even the carrying of curtains was not left to preference; the sanctuary was borne according to a word. Provision for worship: the Persian king decrees that bullocks, rams, lambs, wheat, salt, wine and oil be given “according to the appointment of the priests which are at Jerusalem… day by day without fail” (Ezr 6:9) — a pagan emperor funding the temple at the priests' direction, which is the LORD turning the king's heart whithersoever He will. Murder: “by the appointment of Absalom this hath been determined from the day that he forced his sister Tamar” (2Sa 13:32) — two years of silence, and the whole time a word had been spoken and stood. And friendship: Job's three friends “had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him” (Job 2:11), and they kept it, and sat seven days without speaking, which was the best thing they ever did. Service, provision, murder, and comfort: all settled by an appointment, all standing on somebody's word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines appointment as the act of appointing, designation to office; stipulation, agreement; and decree, established order or constitution.
webster_full: APPOINTMENT, n. The act of appointing; designation to office; as, he erred by the appointment of unsuitable men.
1. Stipulation; agreement; the act of fixing by mutual agreement; as, they made an appointment to meet at six.
2. Decree; established order or constitution; as, it is our duty to submit to the divine appointments.
3. Direction; order; command.
scriptures: Num 4:27

At the appointment of Aaron and his sons shall be all the service of the sons of the Gershonites, in all their burdens, and in all their service: and ye shall appoint unto them in charge all their burdens.
Job 2:11

Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place; Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite: for they had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him.

And Jonadab, the son of Shimeah David's brother, answered and said, Let not my lord suppose that they have slain all the young men the king's sons; for Amnon only is dead: for by the appointment of Absalom this hath been determined from the day that he forced his sister Tamar.
Ezr 6:9

And that which they have need of, both young bullocks, and rams, and lambs, for the burnt offerings of the God of heaven, wheat, salt, wine, and oil, according to the appointment of the priests which are at Jerusalem, let it be given them day by day without fail:
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word means today roughly what it meant in 1611 — an arrangement fixed by a word — though the modern ear hears mainly the calendar sense and misses the older sense of authoritative direction that governs Numbers 4:27 and Ezra 6:9.

The principle to recover is that the service of God is ordered rather than improvised. The Gershonites did not choose which burdens to carry; the appointment came from the priesthood, and the burdens were assigned by name. That instinct stands behind the regulative principle of worship: God is served according to His word and not according to the taste of the servants, and the freedom of a worshipper lies in knowing exactly what he has been given to carry. Job's friends give the pastoral form of the same thing — they made an appointment to come, and they came. Comfort in Scripture is rarely spontaneous; it is usually the keeping of a resolution to show up.
roots_summary: Hebrew peh (H6310), mouth — the idiom at the mouth of, rendered appointment; ya'ad (H3259), to appoint, to meet by agreement; ta'am (H2942), decree.
roots_lines: Hebrew peh (H6310) — mouth; the literal idiom in Numbers 4:27 and 2 Samuel 13:32, at the mouth of Aaron, of Absalom — an order that stands because it was spoken by one with authority.
Hebrew ya'ad (H3259) — to appoint, to fix a time, to meet by agreement; Job 2:11, of the three friends.
Hebrew ta'am (H2942) — decree, command; Ezra 6:9, the Persian decree for the temple's supply.
Hebrew mo'ed (H4150) — an appointed time or meeting; the root of the tabernacle of the congregation, the tent of meeting.
Greek tasso (G5021) — to arrange, appoint, ordain; Acts 13:48, as many as were ordained to eternal life believed.
usage: “At the appointment of Aaron and his sons” — even the curtains were carried by order.
“They had made an appointment together… to comfort him” — and they came.
“By the appointment of Absalom” — two silent years, and a word standing the whole time.
